text.p: Canfor Corp said on Monday that it expects stronger results in 1997 than last year when it lost C$56.9 million or C$0.97 a share.
Chief Executive Arild Nielssen told reporters after the forestry company's annual meeting that Canfor would "definitely do better than last year."
He also said he was "very optimistic for next year, especially on the pulp side."
Despite improving performance in recent quarters, Nielssen told the annual meeting that the company was not satisfied.
"Improving the overall financial return to our shareholders remains our primary goal," he said.

Canfor expects the pulp market to strengthen over the rest of 1997. But Nielssen said pulp price increases are likely to be moderate in the second half of the year because of increased supply from Asia and Latin America.
"Further pulp price improvements are expected in 1998," he said.
Canfor anticipated relatively strong demand for lumber in North America and the Pacific Rim this year.
The company's loss last year stemmed largely from its Howe Sound Pulp and Paper Ltd joint venture with New Oji Paper Co Ltd.

A significant part of Howe Sound's debt matured in the first quarter and was renewed on "favorable terms," Nielssen said. As a result, Canfor does not face the heavy foreign exchange losses it incurred in the previous two years on the debt, he said.
Despite its loss last year, Canfor had cash and credit lines worth about C$250 million at the end of last year, Nielssen said.

Capital spending is projected to rise to C$91 million this year from C$65 million in 1996. This includes carryover of some 1996 expenditures and about C$25 million in funding for a medium-density fiberboard plant in Prince George, British Columbia.

The latter spending is contingent on Canfor finding a new joint venture partner for the plant after a previous partner withdrew and an "ongoing review of the supply-demand situation in the MDF markets," Nielssen said.
Nielssen told reporters that for about a month Canfor has been in discussions with a prospective partner but he declined further comment.
Both Nielssen and Canfor chairman Peter Bentley stressed the importance of winning relief from government-imposed costs and paperwork to the ailing forest industry in British Columbia.

Both said they were optimistic about current discussions underway between the provincial government and forestry companies on the issue. Nielssen said he hoped to see a breakthrough "before the summer."

Nielssen said Canfor is "always looking" at opportunities to become more self sufficient in wood fiber, but he declined to comment on whether Canfor is interested in assets put up for sale by Pacific Forest Products Ltd.
